source_batch.unit_label: CB Module B unit 1: the Reserve Bank of India (courseware unit 4)

facts.statement: Organisational evolution of the Reserve Bank (courseware): the earliest known attempt to set up a bank in India with some characteristics of a modern central banking institution dates back to 1773 on the suggestions of Warren Hastings, Governor of Bengal, the General Bank of Bengal and Bihar, which proved short-lived. Subsequent proposals included Robert Richard Scheme (1807-08), Great Banking Establishment for British India (1836) and National Bank Establishment (by James Wilson in 1860), which remained on paper. The Presidency Banks (Bengal, Bombay and Madras) were quasi-government institutions incorporated under a Charter from the local Government with a share capital part contributed by Government and Government Directors appointed on their boards; the Presidency Bank of Bengal was set up as the Bank of Calcutta (1806) and later called the Bank of Bengal (1809); the Presidency Bank of Bombay and of Madras were established in 1840 and 1843 respectively; they could issue notes up to specified limits until 1862 when with the passing of the Paper Currency Act the sole right to issue notes came to be vested in the Government. Efforts to set up a central bank in India were revived in the early twentieth century in view of public criticism of the currency and exchange system, particularly the Home Charges: payments in sterling by the Government to meet debt, pensions, payments to the War Office; the Fowler Committee considered the issue; several bankers including Alfred de Rothschild emphasised the need for a central bank. The economic conditions of the early years of the twentieth century and the writings of Keynes (the Royal Commission on Indian Finance and Currency, 1913, the Chamberlain Commission, proposed the amalgamation of the three Presidency Banks, and the Imperial Bank of India was formed in 1921). The Imperial Bank performed two central banking functions, banker to government and to some extent bankers bank; other functions like regulation of note issue and management of foreign exchange were not entrusted to it. The Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance (Hilton Young Commission, 1926) recommended the dichotomy of functions and divisions of responsibilities for control of currency and credit be ended and that a central bank called the Reserve Bank of India be established; the Bill to establish the RBI was introduced in January 1927 but there were differences on constitution; a fresh Bill was passed in 1934. The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 came into force on 1 January 1935 (courseware). The Reserve Bank commenced operations on 1 April 1935 as a shareholders institution; the Reserve Bank was nationalised on 1 January 1949 in terms of the Reserve Bank (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948. The core functions of the RBI as laid down in the statutes are: (a) issue of currency, (b) being banker to government, including the function of debt management, and (c) being banker to commercial banks. The Preamble to the RBI Act: to regulate the issue of bank notes and the keeping of reserves with a view to securing monetary stability in India and generally to operate the currency and credit system of the country to its advantage. While most of the central banks were entrusted with traditional functions like note issue, banker to government and bankers bank in their initial years, the RBI was specifically entrusted with an important promotional role to finance agricultural operations and marketing of crops; the Agricultural Credit Department was created simultaneously with the establishment of the RBI in 1935. The rupee was historically linked with pound sterling; it was only in late September 1975 that the rupee was delinked from pound sterling and its value was determined with reference to a basket of currencies until 1991; the exchange rate regime transitioned from a basket linked managed float to a market-based system in March 1993, after a short experiment with a dual exchange rate regime between March 1992 and February 1993. Exchange Control was introduced in India on 3 September 1939; the Bank also provided repatriation of sterling balances; the Banking Companies Act 1949 (renamed the Banking Regulation Act on 1 March 1966).

Development role and institution building (courseware): the Reserve Bank has been seen as a key institution in bringing about development of India; the Bank promoted institutions: the Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI, 1948), State Financial Corporations (1951 Act), Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India (ICICI, 1955), Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI, 1964), the Unit Trust of India (1964), the Agriculture Refinance Corporation (1963) later transformed into the Agriculture Refinance Development Corporation (1974) and finally the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) in 1982, the National Housing Bank (NHB, 1988), the Infrastructure Development Finance Company (IDFC, late 1990s), the Discount and Finance House of India (DFHI, 1988), primary dealers (late 1990s), the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL, 2001), the Board for Regulation and Supervision of Payment and Settlement Systems (BPSS, 2005), the Banking Codes and Standards Board of India (BCSBI, 2006), the National Payments Corporation of India Ltd (NPCI), the Deposit Insurance Corporation (1962) and the Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd (1971). The transformation of the Imperial Bank of India into the State Bank of India (SBI, July 1955) was a major step in expanding the banking network; the seven subsidiaries and associates later; 14 large banks were nationalised in 1969 and six more in 1980 (courseware). Bank nationalisation was largely meant to align banking activities with national concerns and norms: the general inclination in the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s was that Government should become active in promotion of economic activities where it was felt that the private sector was not able or willing to perform. Post nationalisation, the total number of Public Sector Bank branches rose from 8,262 in 1969 to 86,311 in 2021, in rural areas from 1,833 to 28,828; the increased network of branches certainly led to a large expansion of rural credit; the branch expansion of banks in the post-nationalisation period addressed the issue of financial inclusion well before the concept became important in international financial parlance. The Reserve Bank responded quickly to the nationalisation of banks in terms of reorienting its monetary, regulatory and supervisory policies with a view to aligning its activities in line with the goals of nationalisation; it adopted credit planning as a mechanism to ensure the flow of credit to the productive sectors in accordance with plan priorities; the Credit Planning Cell and the Banking Development Cell were established; the Lead Bank Scheme was introduced in 1969. The Reserve Bank had been entrusted with an important promotional role: Rural Banking Enquiry Committee (1949), the All-India Rural Credit Survey (1951), the formation of agricultural refinance; the Reserve Bank Agricultural Credit Department; the Department of Banking Development (1950); the framework of the Directive Principles in the Constitution (1950); the planning process started in April 1951 with the First Five Year Plan; the Planning Commission was established in 1951; the Reserve Bank took the initiative of building the banking network and extending credit to non-banked semi-urban and rural areas; the Industrial Finance (Industrial Finance Department established in 1957 to administer credit guarantee schemes). The Banking Companies Act 1949 was enacted, with the Banking Companies (Amendment) Act, 1950 permitting licensing policy for opening branches outside India; the Reserve Bank established the Department of Non-Banking Supervision of non-banking companies in March 1966 (courseware); the Premises Department set up in 1965; the Legal Division constituted after the Banking Companies Act 1949 and accorded the status of a Legal Department in 1960.

Payments system and cyber security (courseware): the development of a payments system has been undertaken by most central banks; it is recognised that an efficient payment and settlement system is sine qua non for a well-functioning modern financial sector; India pioneered non-cash based payment systems long ago (Hundis). The setting up of a clearing house system in the Presidency towns in the nineteenth century; after the setting up of the Imperial Bank in 1921 settlement was done through cheques drawn on that bank; after the establishment of the RBI in 1935 the Clearing Houses in the Presidency towns were taken over by the Reserve Bank. The Reserve Bank has taken up reforms in the payment and settlement system for more than a decade: the RBI constituted various committees (Rangarajan Committee I and II, Saraf Committee, Patil Committee, etc.) for ICT transformation; from 1998 onwards the RBI has been bringing out a Payment System Vision document, the latest being for the period up to December 2025; recent developments include the Reserve Bank Innovation Hub, a framework for security of card transactions, guidelines on limiting customer liability in unauthorised transactions, Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs), Online Dispute Resolution (ODR), a review of scope and coverage of system audit of Payment System Operators (PSOs), streamlining of Quick Response (QR) code infrastructure, perpetual validity for Certificate of Authorisation of PSOs, and the construction of the RBI Digital Payments Index (DPI). The Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system covering inter-bank transactions was planned and operationalised in March 2004; the RBI delegated MICR cheque processing centres to commercial banks; the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd was set up for clearing and settlement of money, government securities and foreign exchange markets, with the RBI continuing to exercise regulatory oversight. The National Electronic Funds Transfer (NEFT) was initiated by RBI; NEFT is available 24x7x365 from December 2019 and RTGS is available 24x7x365 from 14 December 2020 (courseware); RTGS minimum amount Rs 2 lakh with no upper limit; IMPS is a 24x7 immediate fund transfer facility. The Aadhaar Payments Bridge System (APBS), managed by NPCI, facilitates bulk government benefit and subsidy payments to Aadhaar-seeded bank accounts; the Aadhaar Enabled Payment System (AEPS) facilitates transactions using biometric authentication; RuPay cards, with 321.70 million RuPay cards issued under Prime Minister Jan Dhan accounts by September 2022. Cyber security framework: the RBI issued a comprehensive cyber security framework in June 2016; banks were instructed to put in place a Board approved cyber security policy distinct from the broader IT policy/IS security policy, set up a Security Operations Centre (SOC) for continuous surveillance of cyber threats, address network and database security, protection of customer information, cyber crisis management plan, cyber security preparedness indicators, sharing of information on cyber security incidents with RBI, assessment of gaps in cyber security preparedness, and cyber security awareness stakeholders/top management/board; the RBI also issues advisories and started undertaking cyber security and IT examination of banks separately and integrates the findings into the overall risk assessment under the risk based supervision process.

Relationship with the Government and monetary-fiscal interface (courseware): the RBI is fully owned by the Central Government; Section 7 of the RBI Act 1934 provides the legal backdrop on the role of the Central Government in the management of the affairs of the Bank: sub-section (1) empowers the Central Government to give directions to the Bank in public interest after consultation with the Governor of the Bank; subject to the overarching power given to Central Government to issue directions, the overall control over the affairs of the Bank rests on the Central Board of the Bank (sub-section 2). The RBI is a banker to the Central and State Governments statutorily and by virtue of specific agreements with each of them. Central banks in developing countries have typically financed governments through monetisation; financing has been through automatic monetisation, accompanied by financial repression and erosion of central bank autonomy with respect to monetary policy; in 1951 with the onset of economic planning, the functions of the RBI became more diversified; the RBI played a crucial role in bridging the resource gap of the Government in Five Year Plans through the process of financing government debt by monetisation and maintaining interest rates at artificially low levels (for government securities) to reduce the cost of government borrowing. The provisions of the RBI Act 1934 authorise the RBI to grant advances to the Government, repayable not later than three months from the date of advance; these advances were in principle meant to bridge the temporary mismatches in the Government receipts and expenditure and were mainly intended as tools for Government cash management; in practice the tool of short-term financing became a permanent source of funds for the Government through automatic creation of ad hoc Treasury Bills whenever the Government balances with the RBI fell below the minimum stipulated balance; this automatic monetisation led to the RBI loss of control over creation of reserve money; the ad hoc Treasury Bills continued from the 1950s to the 1990s. By the end of the 1980s a fiscal-monetary-inflation nexus was becoming evident whereby excessive monetary expansion on account of monetisation of fiscal deficit fuelled inflation; the RBI endeavoured to restrict the monetary impact of budgetary imbalances by raising the required reserve ratios to be maintained by banks; as the pre-empted resources were inadequate to meet the Government requirement it had to borrow funds from outside the captive market through postal savings and provident funds by offering substantial financial incentives and at administered low rates of interest, which pushed the economy into the throes of financial repression. An issue of paramount relevance in the central banking arena is the fiscal dominance over monetary policy and its resolution; there was a significant change in thinking regarding the overall economic policy during the early 1990s: a conscious view emerged in favour of fiscal stabilisation and reduction of fiscal deficits aimed at eliminating the dominance of fiscal policy over monetary policy-making in the 1990s; the First Supplemental Agreement between the RBI and the Government of India on 9 September 1994 set out a system of limits for creation of ad hoc Treasury Bills during the three-year period until March 1997; the Second Supplemental Agreement on 6 March 1997 completely phased out the ad hoc Treasury Bills and replaced them by a system of Ways and Means Advances; the participation by the RBI in primary auctions of Government securities has also been discontinued with effect from 1 April 2006 under the provisions of the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003 (FRBM); other related measures included deregulation of interest rates and lowering of statutory liquidity ratios. Box 4.1 (separation of debt management from monetary management: the Indian case): public debt management and monetary policy are vested with the Reserve Bank; the Committee on Capital Account Convertibility (Chairman: S.S. Tarapore, 1997) recommended the separation of debt management from monetary management; the Advisory Group on Transparency in Monetary and Financial Policies recommended it in 2000 but as fiscal responsibility reached a reasonable degree the Reserve Bank, with a Financial Markets Department set up in 2005, functionally separated the debt management and monetary operations; the RBI announces its monetary policy statements bi-monthly (six times in a year) after taking into account the level of market borrowing as announced by the Government in its annual budget; the RBI has developed a Short-Term Liquidity Forecasting Model that projects net liquidity for guiding policy actions in the market on a daily basis; coordination in India is essentially similar in procedure to that between the Treasury and the Federal Reserve Board in the USA; the Reserve Bank of India Act, the Banking Regulation Act amendment permitting flexibility to banks for lowering SLR below 25 per cent of net demand and time liabilities of banks would reduce the captive subscription to Government securities.

Structure and governance of the Reserve Bank (courseware): the Preamble of the RBI Act 1934 stated that the Bank has been constituted to regulate the issue of bank notes and keeping of reserves with a view to securing monetary stability in India and generally to operate the currency and credit system of the country to its advantage; the Act specifies that the Bank is a corporate body with special powers and obligations for serving national interest. Major events that shaped the role of the Reserve Bank (courseware): war financing during the Second World War, planning, the Public Sector enlargement, nationalisation of banks in 1969, the opening up of the economy in 1991, the global economic crisis, the role in the international financial architecture triggered by the IMF, the World Bank and the BIS, and developments in central banking theory and practices. Structure and governance in the 1920s to 1940s: the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance (1926) recommended the transfer of the control of currency and credit functions from the Government and proposed the constitution of a central bank called the Reserve Bank; the Report of the Indian Central Banking Enquiry Committee (1931), followed by the White Paper on Constitutional Reforms (1933), facilitated the execution of the proposal for setting up a Reserve Bank, free from political influences; the India Office Committee Report (IOC, 1933) recommended a shareholders bank to eliminate apprehensions of political interference; the Reserve Bank of India Bill (1933) was adopted as the Reserve Bank of India Act in 1934 in terms of which the Bank commenced operations in April 1935; the Act provided for the constitution of a Central Board of Directors to be entrusted with the general superintendence and direction of the affairs and business of the Bank; the Board consisted of a Governor, two Deputy Governors (appointed by the Governor General-in-Council), four directors (nominated by the Governor General-in-Council), eight directors (elected on behalf of shareholders) and one Government official (nominated by the Governor General-in-Council but with no voting power); the Governor and Deputy Governors were whole-time officers. The Central Government, however, can supersede the Central Board to safeguard against failures of the Board to carry out central banking business entrusted to it; though the Act provided for specific provisions under which the Governor and Deputy Governor could be dismissed, the Central Government reserved the power of dismissal without assigning any reasons or justification for the action; the Act endorsed the establishment of five Local Boards (substituted by four as per the Reserve Bank of India (Amendment) Act No. 11 of 1947 after the termination of Burma Monetary Arrangement) to represent the respective geographical divisions and Local Boards (with members nominated by Central Board) were meant to advise the Central Board on matters referred to them; the Central Board was mandated to hold meetings not less than six times in a year and at least once in every quarter; the Governor presided over these meetings and had a casting vote. The Central Board of Directors held their first meeting on 14 January 1935 in Calcutta; the commencement of the Bank operations on the first day of the fiscal year (April 1, 1935) was a matter of administrative convenience for changeover of Government accounts from the Imperial Bank to the Reserve Bank. The organisational structure of the Bank at the start comprised: (a) Central Office which included Secretary Section, responsible for the secretarial work for the Governor and the Central Board, management of public debt, ways and means requirements of Central and Provincial Governments and matters affecting policies of the Bank, and Chief Accountants Section that maintained and supervised the Bank accounts and included the Issue and Banking Departments dealing with the expenditure matters, remittance of treasure, indent and distribution of notes and coins, besides managing staff, personnel and premises; and (b) Agriculture Credit Department which examined the problems of agricultural credit and also coordinated operations of the Bank with the agencies engaged in extending such credit. The Central Office of the Bank, which was initially located in Kolkata, was permanently shifted to Bombay in December 1937. Inspection Department was constituted in the Central Office as early as 1935 for ensuring internal controls and tightening of the systems and procedures. The Exchange Control Department was constituted in 1939. The Agriculture Credit Department was reorganised in August 1945 into three separate sections: Agriculture Credit, Statistical and Research Section and Banking Section. The Department of Research and Statistics (DRS) in 1945; the Department of Banking Operations. The appointment of Sir C.D. Deshmukh as the first Indian Governor of the RBI on 11 August 1943 and his continuance till end-June 1949. The Banking Companies Act 1949 laid the foundation for legislative framework in terms of which the RBI has been vested with extensive powers of supervision and control over commercial and co-operative banks as well as other financial intermediaries.

Organisational developments and departments (courseware): the Department of Supervision was set up in 1993 (Banking Supervision); the Board for Financial Supervision (BFS) was set up under the aegis of the Reserve Bank in terms of the Reserve Bank of India (BFS) Regulations, 1994; the BFS, chaired by the Governor, has four nominated non-official members from the Central Board of Directors; the Deputy Governors of the Bank are ex-officio members and one of them holding the charge of supervision is appointed as the Vice-Chairman; the Board is empowered to supervise and inspect the whole spectrum of the financial system, viz., banks, Non-Banking Finance Companies (NBFCs), development finance institutions, urban cooperative banks and primary dealers; the Department of Supervision (DoS) was set up in 1993 and assigned the role to function as the executive arm of the BFS. The Securities Department, which came into existence at the inception, was entrusted with purchase and sale of government securities on behalf of the Government. In the wake of the economic reforms program, the Committee on the Financial System (Chairman: M. Narasimham, 1991) made recommendations for the reform of the financial sector. DoS was renamed as the Department of Banking Supervision (DBS) while the Department of Financial Companies (DFC) was renamed as the Department of Non-Banking Supervision (DNBS) in July 1997; a Financial Institutions Division (FID) was set up; the Department of Banking Operations and Development oversaw regulatory functions of commercial banks and para banking institutions; the Rural Planning and Credit Cell (RPCC) was established in 1979 to ensure proper implementation of multi-agent approach to credit disbursal in rural areas; the Industrial Finance Department was established in 1957; the Department of Economic Analysis and Policy (DEAP) and the Department of Statistics and Information Management were set up (Department of Statistics and Information Management formerly DESACS), the Monetary Policy Department (MPD) from 1 January 1998 (formerly the Credit Planning Cell), the Financial Markets Department (FMD) (2005) and the Internal Debt Management Cell (1992) later a Department (IDMD). Monetary policy: Governor Bimal Jalan emphasised the need for fine tuning of monetary policy to the imperatives of the emerging monetary conditions; according to him monetary policy should respond as and when the situation demands; in pursuance of this changed policy stance, the periodicity of monetary policy statements has been revised effective October 1998; quarterly reviews of annual policy statements have been initiated since 2005-06 in place of bi-annual policy statements; a Technical Advisory Committee on monetary policy has also been constituted. Present organisational structure and functions (courseware, as in 2022-23): Consumer Education and Protection Department (CEPD, set up 2006 as Customer Service Department; administers the RB-Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021); Corporate Strategy and Budget Department; Department of Communication (set up from the Press Relations Section in the 1970s, a full-fledged department in March 2007; the RBI communication policy first elaborated in 2008); Department of Regulation (Co-operative Banking) (DCBR, regulates State Co-operative Banks, District Central Co-operative Banks and Urban Co-operative Banks, with dual control with the Registrar of Co-operative Societies); Department of Currency Management (design, printing and supply of notes, circulation of coins, counterfeit notes monitoring, currency chests, note exchange, forged notes vigilance); Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR; publishes the Annual Report and the Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India, State Finances: A Study of Budgets, RBI Bulletin, Handbook of Statistics on Indian Economy and RBI Occasional Papers); Department of External Investments and Operations (DEIO; investment and management of the foreign currency assets and gold of the Reserve Bank, transactions on behalf of Government including with the IMF, membership of BIS); Department of Government and Bank Accounts (DGBA: banker to government and banker to banks: maintains principal deposit accounts of Central and State Governments at the Central Accounts Section, Nagpur, and monitors e-Kuber for direct collection of receipts and making payments); Department of Regulation (Non-Banking) (DNBR; frames policies for regulation and supervision of NBFCs, issues and cancels Certificates of Registration, administers the RBI Act provisions relating to NBFCs and the SARFAESI Act, 2002); Department of Information Technology (DIT; runs NEFT, RTGS (messaging system SFMS) and e-Kuber, has subsidiaries IFTAS and ReBIT); Department of Payment and Settlement Systems (DPSS; set up as a separate department in March 2005; four regional offices; the Board for Regulation and Supervision of Payment and Settlement Systems (BPSS) prescribes policies and meets once every quarter; the PSS Act, 2007 which came into effect from 12 August 2008 prevents any person other than the RBI from operating a payment system unless authorised); Department of Regulation (Banking) (DBR; regulates commercial banks, local area banks and regional rural banks; regulatory oversight of select All India Financial Institutions such as Exim Bank, IDBI, NABARD, NHB and SIDBI and administration of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005); Department of Statistics and Information Management (DSIM; Statistical standards, XBRL, data warehouse); Department of Supervision (supervises scheduled commercial banks (excluding RRBs), local area banks, payments banks, small finance banks, credit information companies, primary urban co-operative banks, NBFCs, asset reconstruction companies and AIFIs; secretariat of BFS and its Sub-Committee and the Inter-Regulatory Forum (IRF) established in 2012; maintains the Central Repository of Information on Large Credits (CRILC); Prompt Corrective Action framework for banks); Enforcement Department (set up in April 2017; the Reserve Bank can impose monetary penalties on regulated entities and not on individuals; from 3 October 2018 it also takes enforcement under Section 58G of the RBI Act; a three-member Committee of Executive Directors adjudicates cases); Financial Inclusion and Development Department (FIDD); Financial Markets Operations Department (FMOD; carved out of FMD in November 2014; LAF (repo, reverse repo, MSF) and OMOs, MSS, forex operations, the 6-currency NEER and REER, secretariat to the Financial Markets Committee (FMC) and the Early Warning Group (EWG); the reference rate for USD/INR has been taken over by Financial Benchmarks India Private Limited (FBIL) with effect from July 10, 2018); Financial Markets Regulation Department (FMRD; set up on 3 November 2014; regulation and development of the money, government securities, foreign exchange markets and related derivatives; financial benchmarks; trade repository for OTC derivatives); Financial Stability Unit (FSU; set up in July 2009; macro-prudential surveillance, the Financial Stability Report, systemic stress tests; the secretariat to the FSDC Sub-Committee, with the Executive Director in charge of FSU as member-secretary); Foreign Exchange Department (FED; FEMA came into force on 1 June 2000 replacing FERA 1973; the RBI is empowered to compound contraventions under Section 15 except Section 3(a)); Human Resource Management Department (HRMD); Inspection Department (set up in 1935; Risk Based Internal Audit (RBIA), Information Systems Audit, Concurrent Audit, Control Self-Assessment Audit (CSAA, at least twice a year), Compliance Audit and Project Audit; ARMS - Audit and Risk Management Sub-Committee of the Central Board; EDC - Executive Directors Committee); Internal Debt Management Department (IDMD; manages the market borrowing programmes of the Government of India and States; Primary Dealers; Public Debt Offices under the Government Securities Act, 2006); International Department (set up on 3 November 2014); Legal Department; Monetary Policy Department (MPD; secretariat to the Monetary Policy Committee, Monetary Policy Report, participates in the Financial Markets Committee, nodal department for lender of last resort, monitors CRR/SLR, authorises food credit to State Governments); Premises Department; Rajbhasha Department; Risk Monitoring Department (RMD; implementation of Enterprise-wide Risk Management System); Secretary Department; Central Vigilance Cell (under the Chief Vigilance Officer).

Salient features of the RBI Act, 1934 (courseware, as amended by the Finance Act 2022): the Act has 61 sections and 2 schedules (sections 59 to 61 repealed; schedules 3 to 5 repealed so the number of schedules reduced to two). Chapter I (Sections 1 and 2): Preliminary: short title, extent and commencement. Chapter II (Sections 3 to 19): establishment and incorporation of Reserve Bank, capital, management (composition of the Central Board, Local Boards, disqualifications of Directors and members of Local Boards (Section 9), meetings of Central Board) and the business which the Bank may transact and not transact. Chapter III (Sections 20 to 45): Central Banking Functions: obligation of the Bank to transact Government business in India (Bank to have the right to transact Government business of States on agreement), right to issue bank notes, transactions in foreign exchange, keeping cash reserves of scheduled banks, publication of consolidated statement by the Bank. Chapter III A (Sections 45A to 45 G): collection and furnishing of credit information. Chapter III B (Sections 45 H to 45 QB): provisions relating to non-banking institutions receiving deposits and financial institutions (definitions, registration and net owned fund, power of Bank to determine policy and issue directions, to collect information from non-banking financial institutions, duty of non-banking institutions to furnish statements, power of Bank to file winding up petition, inspection). Chapter III C (Sections 45R to 45 T): prohibition of acceptance of deposits by unincorporated bodies. Chapter IV (Sections 46 to 58 A): General provisions (contribution by Central Government to the Reserve Bank, contribution to National Rural Credit (Long Term Operations) Fund and National Rural Credit (Stabilization) Fund, National Industrial Credit (Long Term Operations) Fund, National Housing Credit (Long Term Operations) Fund, allocation of surplus profits, publication of Bank Rate, Rural Credit and Development, power of Bank to depute its employees to other institutions, liquidation of the Bank and power of Central Board to make regulations). Chapter V Penalties (Sections 58B to 58G; Sections 59 to 61 repealed): penalties in case of non-compliance. First and Second Schedules: the First Schedule specifies the four areas (Western, Eastern, Northern and Southern) and coverage of States in each area (for Local Boards under Section 9); the Second Schedule (see Section 42 and Section 2(e)) lists names of all Scheduled banks under various categories: State Co-operative Banks, Urban Co-operative Banks, SBI and Associates, Nationalised Banks, Private Banks and Foreign Banks. Principal features: the Bank was constituted for taking over the management of currency from the Central Government and carrying on the business of banking in accordance with the provisions of the Act; the Central Government may from time to time give such directions to the Bank, after consultation with the Governor of the Bank, as it may consider necessary in the public interest; subject to any such directions, the general superintendence and direction of the affairs and business of the Bank shall be entrusted to a Central Board of Directors which may exercise all powers and do all acts and things which may be exercised or done by the Bank. The Central Board shall consist of: (a) a Governor and (not more than four) Deputy Governors to be appointed by the Central Government; (b) four non-official directors to be nominated one each from four local boards; (c) (ten) non-official directors to be nominated by the Central Government; and (d) two Government officials (substituted by Act 12 of 2012 for one Government official, with effect from 1 February 2012) to be nominated by the Central Government. A Local Board shall be constituted for each of the four areas specified in the First Schedule and shall consist of five members to be appointed by the Central Government to represent, as far as possible, the territorial and economic interests of co-operative and indigenous banks; the members of the Local Board shall elect from amongst themselves one person to be the chairman of the Board; every member of a Local Board shall hold office for a term of four years and thereafter until his successor shall have been appointed and shall be eligible for re-appointment; a Local Board shall advise the Central Board on such matters as may be generally or specifically referred to it. The Central Government may remove from office the Governor, or a Deputy Governor or any other Director or any member of Local Board. Meetings of the Central Board shall be convened by the Governor at least six times in each year and at least once in each quarter. If in the opinion of the Central Government the Bank fails to carry out any of the obligations imposed on it by or under this Act, the Central Government may by notification in the Gazette of India declare the Central Board to be superseded, and thereafter the general superintendence and direction of the affairs of the Bank shall be entrusted to such agency as the Central Government may determine; when action is taken under this section the Central Government shall cause a full report of the circumstances leading to such action and of the action taken to be laid before Parliament at the earliest possible opportunity and in any case within three months from the issue of the notification superseding the Board. The Reserve Bank is the sole authority for the issue of currency in India; though one rupee coins/notes and subsidiary coins are issued by the Government of India, they are put into circulation only through the Reserve Bank (Section 22). The issue of Bank notes shall be conducted by the Bank in an Issue Department which shall be separated and kept wholly distinct from the Banking Department, and the assets of the Issue Department shall not be subject to any liability other than the liabilities of the Issue Department. The Issue Department shall not issue bank notes to the Banking Department or to any other person except in exchange for other notes or for such coin, bullion or securities as are permitted by this Act to form part of reserve. The assets of the Issue Department shall consist of gold coin, gold bullion, foreign securities, rupee coin and rupee securities to such aggregate amount as is not less than the total of the liabilities of the Issue Department; the liabilities of the Issue Department shall be an amount equal to the total of the amount of currency notes of the Government of India and bank notes for the time being in circulation. Every bank included in the Second Schedule shall maintain with the Bank an average daily balance the amount of which shall not be less than such per cent of the demand and time liabilities in India as shown in the return referred to in sub-section (2), as the Bank may from time to time, having regard to the needs of securing the monetary stability in the country, notify in the Gazette of India; average daily balance means the average of the balances held at the close of business on each day of the fortnight; fortnight means the period from Saturday to the second following Friday; liabilities shall not include (a) the paid-up capital or the reserves or any credit balance in the profit and loss account, (b) the amount of any loan taken from the Bank or from the Development Bank or from the Exim Bank or from the Reconstruction Bank or from National Housing Bank or from the National Bank or from the Small Industries Bank, and (c) other liabilities as specified in the Act. The Bank may by notification in the Gazette direct that every scheduled bank shall maintain with it an additional average daily balance, which shall in no case be more than the excess of the total of its demand and time liabilities over the total at the close of business on the date specified. If the average daily balance held with the Bank by a scheduled bank during any fortnight is below the minimum prescribed, such Scheduled bank shall be liable to pay to the Bank in respect of that fortnight penal interest at a rate of three per cent above the bank rate on the amount by which such balance with the Bank falls short of the prescribed minimum, and during the next succeeding fortnight the average daily balance is still below the prescribed minimum the rates of penal interest shall be increased to a rate of five per cent above the bank rate. The Bank may collect credit information from banking companies and furnish such information to any banking company with the provisions of Section 45D. The Central Government shall transfer to the Bank rupee securities of the value of five crores of rupees to be allocated by the Bank to the Issue Fund. The Bank shall contribute every year such sums of money as it may consider necessary and feasible to do so to the National Rural Credit (Long Term Operations) Fund and the National Rural Credit (Stabilization) Fund established and maintained by NABARD under Sections 42 and 43 of the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development Act, 1981. The Bank shall establish and maintain a Fund to be known as the National Industrial Credit (Long Term Operations) Fund (initial sum of ten crores of rupees); the Bank shall establish and maintain a Fund to be known as the National Housing Credit (Long Term Operations) Fund. The Bank shall make public from time to time the standard rate at which it is prepared to buy or re-discount bills of exchange or other commercial paper eligible for purchase under this Act (Bank Rate). The Bank shall prepare and transmit to the Central Government a weekly account of the Issue Department and of the Banking Department; within two months from the date on which the annual accounts of the Bank are closed, transmit to the Central Government a copy of the annual accounts signed by the Governor, the Deputy Governors and the Chief Accounting Officer of the Bank, and certified by the auditors, together with a report by the Central Board on the working of the Bank throughout the year. Nothing in the Companies Act, 1956 (as amended in 2013) shall apply to the Bank, and the Bank shall not be placed in liquidation save by order of the Central Government and in such manner as it may direct. Analytics: the RBI functions can be classified into (a) banker to government, (b) issue notes, (c) banker to other banks and (d) maintain the exchange rate. Provision has been made for close co-operation between the Bank and the Government in vital policy-making spheres; the Governor and Deputy Governors; besides Government representation (four directors nominated by the Central Government, Section 8(1)); the day-to-day administration of the Bank affairs is free from Government influence (Section 10(1) and Section 11(5)); the Bank is obliged to accept monies for account of Government at the Centre and for States (Section 20 and Section 21); the credit facilities from the Reserve Bank: discounts and advances against specified instruments under Sections 17(2)(a) and (c), and loans and advances to Scheduled banks and provincial co-operative banks on demand or on expiry of fixed periods not exceeding 90 days against specified securities (Section 17(4)(a) to (d)); instruments of credit control: LAF-Repo rate, Bank Rate and Open Market Operations; Section 49: the Bank shall make public from time to time the standard rate at which it is prepared to buy or rediscount bills of exchange; Section 54: the Bank to create a special Agricultural Credit Department; Section 55: the Bank to make report as early as possible and in any case within three years and to prepare legislation (linking indigenous bankers); Exchange obligation: the Act imposed an obligation on the Reserve Bank to preserve the ruling exchange parity of the rupee at 1s 6d sterling (courseware).

payload.title: Evolution of the Reserve Bank and the idea of a central bank in India
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Early attempts:** the **General Bank of Bengal and Bihar (1773)** under **Warren Hastings** (short-lived); later **proposals** (**1807-08, 1836, 1860**) stayed on paper.

**Presidency Banks:** **Bank of Calcutta (1806)** became **Bank of Bengal (1809)**; **Bombay (1840)** and **Madras (1843)**; they were **quasi-government**, with **Government Directors** and part Government capital. The **Paper Currency Act (1862)** gave **note issue to the Government**.

**Pressure for a central bank:** the **Home Charges** (**sterling payments** by Government for debt, pensions and the War Office) made the **exchange rate** a budget issue; the **Fowler Committee**, **Rothschild's evidence** and **Keynes** pushed the idea; the **Chamberlain Commission (1913)** proposed **merging the three Presidency Banks**, which became the **Imperial Bank of India (1921)**, doing **banker to government** and partly **banker's bank** but **not** note issue or **foreign exchange**.

**Hilton Young Commission (1926)** recommended ending the **dichotomy** between **currency and credit control** and created the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**; Bill of **1927** failed over constitution; fresh **Bill passed in 1934**. The **RBI Act, 1934** took effect from **1 January 1935** (courseware), the **Bank began operations on 1 April 1935** as a **shareholders' bank**, and was **nationalised on 1 January 1949** under the **Reserve Bank (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948**.

**Core functions:** **issue of currency**, **banker to government** (including **debt management**), **banker to commercial banks**. **Preamble:** regulate **note issue** and **keep reserves** to secure **monetary stability** and operate the **currency and credit system** to the country's advantage. From the start the RBI also had a **promotional role** in **agricultural credit** (the **Agricultural Credit Department**, 1935).

**Exchange rate history:** the rupee was linked to **sterling** until **September 1975**, then to a **basket** until **1991**; a **dual rate** (**March 1992 to February 1993**) led to a **market-based system in March 1993**. **Exchange Control** began on **3 September 1939**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The RBI combined note issue, government banking and bankers bank functions with an early developmental task.

payload.title: The developmental role: institutions, nationalisation and credit planning
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Institutions the RBI promoted (courseware):** **IFCI (1948)**, **State Financial Corporations (1951)**, **ICICI (1955)**, **IDBI (1964)**, **UTI (1964)**, **Agricultural Refinance Corporation (1963)** → **Agricultural Refinance Development Corporation (1974)** → **NABARD (1982)**, **NHB (1988)**, **DFHI (1988)**, **IDFC (late 1990s)**, **primary dealers (late 1990s)**, **CCIL (2001)**, **BPSS (2005)**, **BCSBI (2006)**, **NPCI**, the **Deposit Insurance Corporation (1962)** and the **Credit Guarantee Corporation of India (1971)**.

**Banking expansion:** the **Imperial Bank** became **State Bank of India in July 1955**; **14 banks were nationalised in 1969** and **6 more in 1980** to align banking with **national goals** and take credit to **agriculture, small industry and rural areas**. Public sector bank branches rose from **8,262 (1969)** to **86,311 (2021)**; rural branches from **1,833** to **28,828** (dated figures, not taught).

**RBI response to nationalisation:** **credit planning** and the **Credit Planning and Banking Development Cell (1970)**; the **Lead Bank Scheme (1969)**; monitoring **priority sector** credit; the **Rural Banking Enquiry Committee (1949)** and **All-India Rural Credit Survey (1951)**; the **Department of Banking Development (1950)**; **Industrial Finance Department (1957)**; the **Banking Companies Act, 1949** (renamed **Banking Regulation Act, 1966**) and the **1950 and 1959 amendments** extending the Act's coverage to branches abroad and foreign branches; non-banking supervision created in **March 1966**.

**Context:** the **Planning Commission** and the **First Five Year Plan (1951)** made **financial development a tool for plan priorities**.

payload.title: Payment and settlement systems and cyber security
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Why:** an efficient payment and settlement system is **essential for a modern financial sector**. India had used **hundis** (the credit instrument) for centuries.

**Clearing history:** **clearing houses** in the **Presidency towns** (19th century) → settlement via the **Imperial Bank (1921)** → **RBI took over** after **1935**.

**Reform programme:** committees (**Rangarajan I and II**, **Saraf**, **Patil**) and **Payment System Vision** documents from **1998** (latest to **December 2025**); recent steps: **RBI Innovation Hub**, **security of card transactions**, **limiting customer liability**, **Prepaid Payment Instruments**, **Online Dispute Resolution**, **system audit of PSOs**, **QR code** streamlining, **perpetual authorisation** for PSOs and the **RBI Digital Payments Index**.

**Systems:** **RTGS** (operationalised **March 2004**; **24x7 from 14 December 2020**; minimum **Rs 2 lakh**), **NEFT** (**24x7 from December 2019**), **IMPS** (24x7 instant), **APBS** (Aadhaar-seeded bulk **government benefit** payments, run by **NPCI**), **AEPS** (**biometric** Aadhaar payments) and **RuPay**. **CCIL** clears **money, government securities and forex** trades; the RBI keeps **settlement and oversight**.

**Cyber security framework (June 2016):** a **Board-approved cyber security policy** separate from the IT policy; a **Security Operations Centre (SOC)** for **continuous surveillance**; **network and database security**; **customer information protection**; a **cyber crisis management plan**; **preparedness indicators**; **reporting incidents to the RBI**; **gap assessment**; and **awareness**. The RBI also **examines IT and cyber security** and feeds this into **risk based supervision**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Payment systems and cyber security are now core supervisory topics because failure spreads quickly.

payload.title: Relationship with the Government and the monetary-fiscal interface
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Ownership and control:** the RBI is **fully owned by the Central Government**. **Section 7(1)** lets the Government give **directions in the public interest** after **consulting the Governor**; subject to that, the **Central Board** controls the affairs (**Section 7(2)**). The RBI is **banker to Central and State Governments** by **statute and agreements**.

**Monetisation history:** with **planning from 1951** the RBI helped **bridge the Government's resource gap** by **financing government debt** through **monetisation** and keeping **government security yields artificially low**. **Section 17** allows **advances to the Government repayable within three months** for **cash management**, but in practice **ad hoc Treasury Bills** created **automatic monetisation** from the **1950s to the 1990s**, so the RBI **lost control over reserve money**.

**Fiscal-monetary-inflation nexus:** by the late **1980s** excess monetary expansion fed **inflation**; the RBI **raised reserve ratios**; the Government borrowed from **captive sources** at **administered rates**: **financial repression**.

**Reforms:** early **1990s** shift to **fiscal stabilisation**; **9 September 1994** First Supplemental Agreement set **limits on ad hocs** for **three years**; **6 March 1997** Supplemental Agreement **phased out ad hocs** (replaced by **Ways and Means Advances**); the RBI stopped taking part in **primary auctions from 1 April 2006** under the **FRBM Act, 2003**; **SLR was lowered**; **interest rates were deregulated**.

**Debt management debate (Box 4.1):** the **Tarapore Committee (1997)** and the **Advisory Group on Transparency (2000)** favoured **separating debt management** from monetary policy; in India the RBI instead set up a **Financial Markets Department (2005)** to **separate operations functionally**; **monetary policy statements** are announced **bi-monthly** after considering the **Government's market borrowing**; a **Short-Term Liquidity Forecasting Model** projects **net liquidity daily**. Coordination resembles the **US Treasury-Federal Reserve** arrangement.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: India separated the functions inside the RBI rather than moving debt management out of it.

payload.title: Structure and governance of the Reserve Bank in the early years
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Origins of the governance structure:** the **Hilton Young Commission (1926)**, the **Indian Central Banking Enquiry Committee (1931)**, the **White Paper on Constitutional Reforms (1933)** and the **India Office Committee (1933)** (which recommended a **shareholders' bank** to avoid **political interference**) led to the **1934 Act**.

**Original Central Board:** a **Governor**, **two Deputy Governors** (appointed by the Governor General in Council), **four nominated directors**, **eight elected directors** (by shareholders) and **one Government official without a vote**; the **Governor and Deputy Governors were whole-time**. The **Government could supersede the Board** and **dismiss the Governor** without giving reasons. **Five Local Boards** were reduced to **four** by **the 1947 Amendment** (after the **Burma Monetary Arrangement ended**). The Board met **at least six times a year, once a quarter**; the **Governor presided** with a **casting vote**.

**Start:** **first Board meeting 14 January 1935, Calcutta**; operations began **1 April 1935** (first day of the fiscal year, for **changeover of Government accounts** from the Imperial Bank); **Central Office moved from Calcutta to Bombay in December 1937**.

**Early structure:** **Central Office** (Secretary's Section; Chief Accountant's Section with **Issue** and **Banking Departments**), the **Agricultural Credit Department**, the **Inspection Department (1935)**, the **Exchange Control Department (1939)**, **Department of Research and Statistics (1945)**. **Sir C.D. Deshmukh** became the **first Indian Governor on 11 August 1943** (till **June 1949**).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The shareholders bank model was meant to protect the central bank from political interference.

payload.title: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934: structure and salient features
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Chapters:** **I** (Sections 1-2) preliminary; **II** (3-19) incorporation, capital, **management** (Central Board, Local Boards, disqualifications, meetings) and **business the Bank may or may not transact**; **III** (20-45) **central banking functions** (Government business, **note issue**, **foreign exchange**, **cash reserves of scheduled banks**); **III A** (45A-45G) **credit information**; **III B** (45H-45QB) **non-banking institutions receiving deposits**; **III C** (45R-45T) **unincorporated bodies' deposits**; **IV** (46-58A) **general provisions** (funds, **Bank Rate publication**, surplus, regulations); **V** (58B-58G) **penalties**. **Schedules:** **First** (the four areas for Local Boards) and **Second** (**scheduled banks**).

**Central Board:** a **Governor** and up to **four Deputy Governors**; **four non-official directors** (one from each Local Board); **ten non-official directors** nominated by the Government; **two Government officials** (from **1 February 2012**). The Government can **remove** the Governor, a Deputy Governor or any director, and **supersede the Board** by notification if the Bank fails its obligations (a report to **Parliament within three months**). The Board meets **at least six times a year and once each quarter**.

**Local Boards:** one for each of the **four areas**, **five members** each, **four-year term**, advise the Central Board.

**Note issue (Section 22):** the RBI is the **sole authority**; **rupee coins and one-rupee notes** are issued by the **Government** but circulate **only through the RBI**. The **Issue Department** is **separate** from the **Banking Department** and its assets (**gold, foreign securities, rupee coin and rupee securities**) must at least equal its liabilities (**notes in circulation**).

**Cash reserve (Section 42):** each **scheduled bank** keeps an **average daily balance** at a **notified percentage** of its **demand and time liabilities** (the fortnight runs **Saturday to the second following Friday**); additional balances may be prescribed; **penal interest** of **3 per cent above the Bank Rate**, **5 per cent** if the shortfall continues.

**Other provisions:** **credit information** (**Section 45D**); **Bank Rate** (**Section 49**); **Agricultural Credit Department** (**Section 54**); **weekly accounts** of the Issue and Banking Departments; **annual accounts** within **two months**, signed by the **Governor, Deputy Governors and Chief Accounting Officer**; the **Companies Act does not apply**; the Bank can be **liquidated only by Government order**; funds: **National Rural Credit (LTO and Stabilization)**, **National Industrial Credit (LTO)** and **National Housing Credit (LTO)**.

**Functions in the Act:** **banker to government**, **issue of notes**, **banker to banks** and **maintaining the exchange rate**; credit facilities under **Section 17**; credit control by **LAF-repo**, **Bank Rate** and **OMOs**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The Act ties the Bank to the Government through directions and the Board but protects day-to-day administration from influence.

items.title: Evolution of the Reserve Bank and the idea of a central bank in India
items.core_explanation_md:
**Early attempts:** the **General Bank of Bengal and Bihar (1773)** under **Warren Hastings** (short-lived); later **proposals** (**1807-08, 1836, 1860**) stayed on paper.

**Presidency Banks:** **Bank of Calcutta (1806)** became **Bank of Bengal (1809)**; **Bombay (1840)** and **Madras (1843)**; they were **quasi-government**, with **Government Directors** and part Government capital. The **Paper Currency Act (1862)** gave **note issue to the Government**.

**Pressure for a central bank:** the **Home Charges** (**sterling payments** by Government for debt, pensions and the War Office) made the **exchange rate** a budget issue; the **Fowler Committee**, **Rothschild's evidence** and **Keynes** pushed the idea; the **Chamberlain Commission (1913)** proposed **merging the three Presidency Banks**, which became the **Imperial Bank of India (1921)**, doing **banker to government** and partly **banker's bank** but **not** note issue or **foreign exchange**.

**Hilton Young Commission (1926)** recommended ending the **dichotomy** between **currency and credit control** and created the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**; Bill of **1927** failed over constitution; fresh **Bill passed in 1934**. The **RBI Act, 1934** took effect from **1 January 1935** (courseware), the **Bank began operations on 1 April 1935** as a **shareholders' bank**, and was **nationalised on 1 January 1949** under the **Reserve Bank (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948**.

**Core functions:** **issue of currency**, **banker to government** (including **debt management**), **banker to commercial banks**. **Preamble:** regulate **note issue** and **keep reserves** to secure **monetary stability** and operate the **currency and credit system** to the country's advantage. From the start the RBI also had a **promotional role** in **agricultural credit** (the **Agricultural Credit Department**, 1935).

**Exchange rate history:** the rupee was linked to **sterling** until **September 1975**, then to a **basket** until **1991**; a **dual rate** (**March 1992 to February 1993**) led to a **market-based system in March 1993**. **Exchange Control** began on **3 September 1939**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The RBI combined note issue, government banking and bankers bank functions with an early developmental task.

items.title: The developmental role: institutions, nationalisation and credit planning
items.core_explanation_md:
**Institutions the RBI promoted (courseware):** **IFCI (1948)**, **State Financial Corporations (1951)**, **ICICI (1955)**, **IDBI (1964)**, **UTI (1964)**, **Agricultural Refinance Corporation (1963)** → **Agricultural Refinance Development Corporation (1974)** → **NABARD (1982)**, **NHB (1988)**, **DFHI (1988)**, **IDFC (late 1990s)**, **primary dealers (late 1990s)**, **CCIL (2001)**, **BPSS (2005)**, **BCSBI (2006)**, **NPCI**, the **Deposit Insurance Corporation (1962)** and the **Credit Guarantee Corporation of India (1971)**.

**Banking expansion:** the **Imperial Bank** became **State Bank of India in July 1955**; **14 banks were nationalised in 1969** and **6 more in 1980** to align banking with **national goals** and take credit to **agriculture, small industry and rural areas**. Public sector bank branches rose from **8,262 (1969)** to **86,311 (2021)**; rural branches from **1,833** to **28,828** (dated figures, not taught).

**RBI response to nationalisation:** **credit planning** and the **Credit Planning and Banking Development Cell (1970)**; the **Lead Bank Scheme (1969)**; monitoring **priority sector** credit; the **Rural Banking Enquiry Committee (1949)** and **All-India Rural Credit Survey (1951)**; the **Department of Banking Development (1950)**; **Industrial Finance Department (1957)**; the **Banking Companies Act, 1949** (renamed **Banking Regulation Act, 1966**) and the **1950 and 1959 amendments** extending the Act's coverage to branches abroad and foreign branches; non-banking supervision created in **March 1966**.

**Context:** the **Planning Commission** and the **First Five Year Plan (1951)** made **financial development a tool for plan priorities**.

items.title: Payment and settlement systems and cyber security
items.core_explanation_md:
**Why:** an efficient payment and settlement system is **essential for a modern financial sector**. India had used **hundis** (the credit instrument) for centuries.

**Clearing history:** **clearing houses** in the **Presidency towns** (19th century) → settlement via the **Imperial Bank (1921)** → **RBI took over** after **1935**.

**Reform programme:** committees (**Rangarajan I and II**, **Saraf**, **Patil**) and **Payment System Vision** documents from **1998** (latest to **December 2025**); recent steps: **RBI Innovation Hub**, **security of card transactions**, **limiting customer liability**, **Prepaid Payment Instruments**, **Online Dispute Resolution**, **system audit of PSOs**, **QR code** streamlining, **perpetual authorisation** for PSOs and the **RBI Digital Payments Index**.

**Systems:** **RTGS** (operationalised **March 2004**; **24x7 from 14 December 2020**; minimum **Rs 2 lakh**), **NEFT** (**24x7 from December 2019**), **IMPS** (24x7 instant), **APBS** (Aadhaar-seeded bulk **government benefit** payments, run by **NPCI**), **AEPS** (**biometric** Aadhaar payments) and **RuPay**. **CCIL** clears **money, government securities and forex** trades; the RBI keeps **settlement and oversight**.

**Cyber security framework (June 2016):** a **Board-approved cyber security policy** separate from the IT policy; a **Security Operations Centre (SOC)** for **continuous surveillance**; **network and database security**; **customer information protection**; a **cyber crisis management plan**; **preparedness indicators**; **reporting incidents to the RBI**; **gap assessment**; and **awareness**. The RBI also **examines IT and cyber security** and feeds this into **risk based supervision**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Payment systems and cyber security are now core supervisory topics because failure spreads quickly.

items.title: Relationship with the Government and the monetary-fiscal interface
items.core_explanation_md:
**Ownership and control:** the RBI is **fully owned by the Central Government**. **Section 7(1)** lets the Government give **directions in the public interest** after **consulting the Governor**; subject to that, the **Central Board** controls the affairs (**Section 7(2)**). The RBI is **banker to Central and State Governments** by **statute and agreements**.

**Monetisation history:** with **planning from 1951** the RBI helped **bridge the Government's resource gap** by **financing government debt** through **monetisation** and keeping **government security yields artificially low**. **Section 17** allows **advances to the Government repayable within three months** for **cash management**, but in practice **ad hoc Treasury Bills** created **automatic monetisation** from the **1950s to the 1990s**, so the RBI **lost control over reserve money**.

**Fiscal-monetary-inflation nexus:** by the late **1980s** excess monetary expansion fed **inflation**; the RBI **raised reserve ratios**; the Government borrowed from **captive sources** at **administered rates**: **financial repression**.

**Reforms:** early **1990s** shift to **fiscal stabilisation**; **9 September 1994** First Supplemental Agreement set **limits on ad hocs** for **three years**; **6 March 1997** Supplemental Agreement **phased out ad hocs** (replaced by **Ways and Means Advances**); the RBI stopped taking part in **primary auctions from 1 April 2006** under the **FRBM Act, 2003**; **SLR was lowered**; **interest rates were deregulated**.

**Debt management debate (Box 4.1):** the **Tarapore Committee (1997)** and the **Advisory Group on Transparency (2000)** favoured **separating debt management** from monetary policy; in India the RBI instead set up a **Financial Markets Department (2005)** to **separate operations functionally**; **monetary policy statements** are announced **bi-monthly** after considering the **Government's market borrowing**; a **Short-Term Liquidity Forecasting Model** projects **net liquidity daily**. Coordination resembles the **US Treasury-Federal Reserve** arrangement.

items.title: Structure and governance of the Reserve Bank in the early years
items.core_explanation_md:
**Origins of the governance structure:** the **Hilton Young Commission (1926)**, the **Indian Central Banking Enquiry Committee (1931)**, the **White Paper on Constitutional Reforms (1933)** and the **India Office Committee (1933)** (which recommended a **shareholders' bank** to avoid **political interference**) led to the **1934 Act**.

**Original Central Board:** a **Governor**, **two Deputy Governors** (appointed by the Governor General in Council), **four nominated directors**, **eight elected directors** (by shareholders) and **one Government official without a vote**; the **Governor and Deputy Governors were whole-time**. The **Government could supersede the Board** and **dismiss the Governor** without giving reasons. **Five Local Boards** were reduced to **four** by **the 1947 Amendment** (after the **Burma Monetary Arrangement ended**). The Board met **at least six times a year, once a quarter**; the **Governor presided** with a **casting vote**.

**Start:** **first Board meeting 14 January 1935, Calcutta**; operations began **1 April 1935** (first day of the fiscal year, for **changeover of Government accounts** from the Imperial Bank); **Central Office moved from Calcutta to Bombay in December 1937**.

**Early structure:** **Central Office** (Secretary's Section; Chief Accountant's Section with **Issue** and **Banking Departments**), the **Agricultural Credit Department**, the **Inspection Department (1935)**, the **Exchange Control Department (1939)**, **Department of Research and Statistics (1945)**. **Sir C.D. Deshmukh** became the **first Indian Governor on 11 August 1943** (till **June 1949**).

items.title: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934: structure and salient features
items.core_explanation_md:
**Chapters:** **I** (Sections 1-2) preliminary; **II** (3-19) incorporation, capital, **management** (Central Board, Local Boards, disqualifications, meetings) and **business the Bank may or may not transact**; **III** (20-45) **central banking functions** (Government business, **note issue**, **foreign exchange**, **cash reserves of scheduled banks**); **III A** (45A-45G) **credit information**; **III B** (45H-45QB) **non-banking institutions receiving deposits**; **III C** (45R-45T) **unincorporated bodies' deposits**; **IV** (46-58A) **general provisions** (funds, **Bank Rate publication**, surplus, regulations); **V** (58B-58G) **penalties**. **Schedules:** **First** (the four areas for Local Boards) and **Second** (**scheduled banks**).

**Central Board:** a **Governor** and up to **four Deputy Governors**; **four non-official directors** (one from each Local Board); **ten non-official directors** nominated by the Government; **two Government officials** (from **1 February 2012**). The Government can **remove** the Governor, a Deputy Governor or any director, and **supersede the Board** by notification if the Bank fails its obligations (a report to **Parliament within three months**). The Board meets **at least six times a year and once each quarter**.

**Local Boards:** one for each of the **four areas**, **five members** each, **four-year term**, advise the Central Board.

**Note issue (Section 22):** the RBI is the **sole authority**; **rupee coins and one-rupee notes** are issued by the **Government** but circulate **only through the RBI**. The **Issue Department** is **separate** from the **Banking Department** and its assets (**gold, foreign securities, rupee coin and rupee securities**) must at least equal its liabilities (**notes in circulation**).

**Cash reserve (Section 42):** each **scheduled bank** keeps an **average daily balance** at a **notified percentage** of its **demand and time liabilities** (the fortnight runs **Saturday to the second following Friday**); additional balances may be prescribed; **penal interest** of **3 per cent above the Bank Rate**, **5 per cent** if the shortfall continues.

**Other provisions:** **credit information** (**Section 45D**); **Bank Rate** (**Section 49**); **Agricultural Credit Department** (**Section 54**); **weekly accounts** of the Issue and Banking Departments; **annual accounts** within **two months**, signed by the **Governor, Deputy Governors and Chief Accounting Officer**; the **Companies Act does not apply**; the Bank can be **liquidated only by Government order**; funds: **National Rural Credit (LTO and Stabilization)**, **National Industrial Credit (LTO)** and **National Housing Credit (LTO)**.

**Functions in the Act:** **banker to government**, **issue of notes**, **banker to banks** and **maintaining the exchange rate**; credit facilities under **Section 17**; credit control by **LAF-repo**, **Bank Rate** and **OMOs**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Act ties the Bank to the Government through directions and the Board but protects day-to-day administration from influence.
